match_note: The file covers only the Nature Communications rounds; the manuscript had already been reviewed and revised at another journal (Reviewer 1 says so and refers to an earlier response letter). The reviewed version shares v1's core content (trilayer and superlattice samples, +5 V trailing fields, ~1170 nm displacement, +17 V in-situ STEM with a tungsten tip, vortex rings under pulsed fields), but it claims 'topologically protected' motion, reports displacements up to ~3000-3100 nm, invokes coupling of net in-plane polarization to an in-plane trailing field, and states a 3.9574 A PbTiO3 reference lattice parameter; none of these appear in v1 (titled 'Harnessing the polar vortex motion in oxide heterostructures'), and the STEM panel is Fig. 2i rather than v1's Fig. 2j.

concerns.quote: the authors repeatedly equate vortex boundary displacement with the motion of polar vortices... The core claim of this work — controlled motion of polar vortices — is not achieved as stated.
concerns.summary: The data show displacement of boundaries between zig-zag and near-flat vortex arrangements (a vertical reconfiguration), not translational motion of vortices, so the central claim is unsupported.

concerns.quote: the novelty of this work is insufficient. A number of prior publications have already reported field-induced motion and dynamics of polar vortices
concerns.summary: Field-induced motion and dynamics of polar vortices were already reported (Sci. Adv. 2022, Acta Mater. 2018), so the advance is unclear.

concerns.quote: they never clarify how the polar vortices gain topological protection during the movement
concerns.summary: The claim of topologically protected motion is unjustified because ferroelectric vortices lack the DMI-type stabilization of magnetic textures.
concerns.response: addressed with new data or analysis

concerns.quote: To validate the proposed mechanism, dedicated in-situ experiments with pure in-plane electric fields are strongly required
concerns.summary: The proposed mechanism relies on an in-plane field coupling to net in-plane polarization, but the in-situ STEM field is out-of-plane; a pure in-plane-field experiment is needed.

concerns.quote: The LPFM signals merely reflect the shift of transition boundaries, and cannot be used to quantify the translational moving distance of vortices.
concerns.summary: In the superlattice with coexisting a1/a2 domains, the field only triggers a transition and LPFM cannot measure vortex travel distance.

concerns.quote: Readers will struggle to comprehend the five intricate figures composed of numerous sub-panels, which cover two different sample systems simultaneously.
concerns.summary: The paper is overloaded; the mixed-phase superlattice sample distracts from the message and the figures should be reorganised around the trilayer only.

concerns.quote: Could the authors justify why they consider rather 3.9574 A for bulk PbTiO3 and thus compressive strain when PbTio3 is grown on DyScO3?
concerns.summary: The PbTiO3 lattice parameter used implies compressive rather than the expected tensile strain on DyScO3, which may change the phase-field predictions.

concerns.quote: an electric field of such magnitude is strong enough to destroy polar vortex structures. It is confusing why only vortex reconfiguration rather than vortex annihilation was observed
concerns.summary: A 17 V bias from a sub-10 nm tip should annihilate vortices, so observing only reconfiguration is puzzling.

concerns.quote: the authors do not specify the radius of the tungsten probe.
concerns.summary: The tungsten probe radius for the in-situ STEM biasing is not given.

concerns.quote: Only initial and final states before and after bias application are presented; the full dynamic evolution process is missing
concerns.summary: The in-situ STEM shows only before and after states, not the dynamic evolution under bias.

later_concerns.quote: That the boundaries of the vortices are the mobile objects... does not appear to be a great finding to me
later_concerns.summary: Round 2: after retitling to boundary motion, the finding has mainly academic relevance; still recommends publication.
